newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany seeks to nail Bormann rumours with DNA.
newsitem.headline: Germany seeks to nail Bormann rumours with DNA.

text.p: German prosecutors are seeking to lay to rest once and for all rumours surrounding the possible escape of Martin Bormann, Adolf Hitler's infamous top henchman, by carrying out DNA tests on the skeleton thought to be his.
Bormann, who stayed close to Hitler until the last few days of the Third Reich, is thought to have died either at the hands of Russian snipers or by committing suicide.

But interest in his fate was revived last year by a British book that asserted Bormann was spirited away after the war by British commandos in a bid to get him to release Nazi gold held in Swiss banks.

The emergence of a Uruguayan passport allegedly used by Bormann to flee to Argentina further added to the mystery surrounding the war criminal who was sentenced to death in absentia at the Nuremberg trials.

"Time and time again there are claims that the top Nazis escaped, which of course some of them did," Hildegard Becker-Toussaint, chief prosecutor in the central German state of Hesse, told Reuters on Tuesday.

Becker-Toussaint, whose state is conducting the analysis because Bormann still faces murder charges there, said it was already virtually certain that a corpse unearthed on a Berlin building site over 20 years ago was Bormann's.
Dental records and injuries found on that skeleton have already been matched successfully with records held on Bormann, who acted as Hitler's deputy and main confidant.
Moreover, a reconstruction of facial features that was based on the corpse's skull also supported the theory that Bormann's body had been found, she said.
But she said it was hoped the new study will prove once and for all the skeleton does belong to Bormann by using technology able to analyse DNA from body parts that have already long been dead.
DNA is the genetic "code" that determines the unique features of living creatures and is widely seen as incontestible proof of identity.
Because of the peculiarities of the testing method used, the conclusiveness of the analysis will rely on the results then being compared to the DNA of a living, female relative of Bormann.

Becker-Toussaint did not say whether a member of Borman's family had already been identified and approached to corroborate the test results but said the whole process was likely to take "months rather than weeks".

Controversy was provoked last September by a book whose author, Christopher Creighton, insisted he was second-in-command of a 300-strong commando unit led by James Bond creator Ian Fleming to save Bormann from the gallows.

The ultimate aim of the British unit was to bring Bormann to London and get his signature on documents releasing Nazi gold held in Swiss banks, the author of the book "Operation James Bond" suggested.
The book met with such scepticism that its publishers issued a 20,000 pound sterling challenge in national newspapers to anyone who could prove that "Operation James Bond" did not take place.
Another British writer came forward to claim the reward, insisting he had evidence that no such operation existed, but the author of the book stuck by his assertion that the rescue did take place.

Speculation about what happened to Bormann has been further heightened following the discovery last year of a passport issued in 1946 by the Uruguayan consulate in the Italian city of Genoa to one Ricardo Bauer.
The name of Bauer was allegedly an alias used by Bormann in his escape to Argentina after the war.
